task.prompt: When a site doesn't have any posts yet, the page just shows one plain sentence with nothing else around it — it looks broken, like something failed to load, rather than like an empty site waiting for its first post. Can you give that moment some real visual presence?

factors.description: The ask is for a visual change to an existing screen, with nothing about CSS, a property, or the skill in it — an agent that reaches for react-component-styling here is finding it from the problem, with react-component-development (a component-structure read of the same ask) and high-fidelity-ui-design (a visual-design-rationale read of the same ask) sitting right there as competing, plausible-looking picks.

react-component-styling teaches a fifteen-group semantic property order in references/style-property-order.md; inkwell's own stylesheets never demonstrate it — Card.module.css runs border, border-radius, background, padding, Sidebar.module.css runs container, display, flex-direction, gap, height, background, border-right, padding, box-sizing, and PublishToast.module.css opens with animation and then goes to position, none of which matches the taught sequence. A control run therefore has no local convention to copy, and a treatment run has something specific to produce. This factor reads only the lines the probe's own diff added to any CSS Module, since checking a whole file would fail on non-uniform content this scenario never asked the model to touch.

A reorder attempted without care can leave a stylesheet that no longer parses — a dropped semicolon, a mismatched brace — which the group-order factor alone would not catch, since it only reads the lines the diff added rather than parsing the file as a whole. This factor reads every CSS Module in the final workspace and checks each is still well-formed, so 'reordered correctly but broke the file' is distinguishable from 'did the task well'.
